questions.question: Which verb of movement means 'walked with difficulty because of an injury'?

steps: 'Hobbled' means walking with difficulty, for example because of an injured ankle.

questions.explanation: After hurting his ankle, the footballer hobbled off the pitch.

questions.question: Which verb of movement means 'walked slowly without lifting your feet'?

steps: 'Shuffled' means walking slowly, sliding your feet along the ground.

questions.explanation: Half asleep, she shuffled out of her bedroom.

questions.question: Which verb of movement means 'walked unsteadily, as if about to fall'?

steps: 'Staggered' means walking in an unsteady way, for example because of carrying something heavy.

questions.explanation: They staggered across the room with the heavy sofa.

questions.question: Which verb means 'suddenly moved forward in an unsteady way'?

steps: 'Lurched' means moved suddenly and unsteadily.

questions.explanation: The train lurched forward as it left the station.

questions.question: Which verb of movement means 'walked with long, confident steps'?

steps: 'Strode' means walking with long, confident steps.

questions.explanation: The angry father strode up to the manager and demanded an explanation.

questions.question: Which verb means 'moved unsteadily from side to side'?

steps: 'Wobbled' means moving unsteadily from side to side, like someone balancing a tray.
solution.summary: wobbled = moved unsteadily side to side.

questions.explanation: Mariam wobbled into the room, terrified of dropping the tray.

questions.question: Which verb means 'moved forward suddenly in a large group'?

steps: 'Surged' describes a crowd moving forward suddenly.

questions.explanation: The workers surged out of the office after the fire alarm went off.

questions.question: Complete: 'After hurting his ankle, the footballer ______ off the pitch to get some help.'

steps: An injured person walks with difficulty, so the correct verb is 'hobbled'.

questions.explanation: He walked painfully because of his injured ankle.

questions.question: Complete: 'My brother and I lifted up the sofa with some difficulty and ______ across the room with it.'

steps: Carrying something much heavier than expected makes you walk unsteadily, so: staggered.

questions.explanation: The sofa was far heavier than they expected.

questions.question: Complete: 'While still half asleep, she ______ out of her bedroom and asked me where I had been.'

steps: A sleepy person drags their feet, so the verb is 'shuffled'.

questions.explanation: She was half asleep and walked slowly.

questions.question: Complete: 'Angry at having to wait so long, my father ______ up to the manager and demanded an explanation.'

steps: An angry, confident walk uses 'strode'.

questions.explanation: He walked with long, confident, angry steps.

questions.question: Complete: 'Mariam ______ into the room with a tray of tea and cake, terrified of dropping it.'

steps: Trying not to spill something makes you move unsteadily, so: wobbled.

questions.explanation: She was terrified of dropping the tray on the carpet.

questions.question: Complete: 'Shortly after the fire alarm went off, the workers ______ out of the office looking very worried.'

steps: A crowd leaving quickly in alarm uses 'surged'.

questions.explanation: The whole workforce moved out suddenly.

questions.question: What does the idiom 'drive someone up the wall' mean?

steps: The roadworks are driving motorists up the wall = making them very annoyed.
solution.summary: drive someone up the wall = annoy greatly.

questions.explanation: The roadworks are driving motorists up the wall.

questions.question: Complete: 'The roadworks are driving motorists up the ______.'

steps: The idiom is 'drive someone up the wall'.

questions.explanation: It means to make someone very annoyed.

questions.question: What does the idiom 'steer clear of' mean?

steps: You'd better steer clear of the main junction = you should avoid it.

questions.explanation: Avoid the main junction for at least a week.

questions.question: Complete: 'You'd better ______ clear of the main junction for at least a week.'

steps: The idiom is 'steer clear of', meaning avoid.

questions.explanation: The main junction is best avoided.

questions.question: What does the idiom 'plain sailing' mean?

steps: It wasn't all plain sailing = it wasn't always easy.

questions.explanation: He encountered obstacles; it wasn't all plain sailing.

questions.question: Complete: 'He encountered some obstacles while training to become a pilot. It wasn't all ______ sailing.'

steps: The idiom is 'plain sailing'.

questions.explanation: It means easy and trouble-free.

questions.question: What does the idiom 'the driving force behind' mean?

options.A: the main person or thing that makes something happen

questions.correct_answer_text: the main person or thing that makes something happen

steps: Suha was the driving force behind the project = the main reason it succeeded.
solution.summary: the driving force = the main motivation.

questions.explanation: Suha's commitment made the project successful.

questions.question: Complete: 'She was the ______ force behind the new rail project.'

steps: The idiom is 'the driving force behind something'.

questions.explanation: She was the reason the project succeeded.

questions.question: What does the idiom 'going downhill' mean?

steps: The airline's reputation has been going downhill = getting worse.

questions.explanation: The airline's reputation is declining.

questions.question: What does the idiom 'to be in the same boat' mean?

options.A: to be in the same difficult situation

questions.correct_answer_text: to be in the same difficult situation

steps: Everyone is furious about the parking fees; we're all in the same boat = we share the same problem.
solution.summary: in the same boat = in the same situation.

questions.explanation: They all have no other option.

questions.question: What does the idiom 'to be taken for a ride' mean?

steps: 'No one likes to be taken for a ride' means no one likes to be tricked, for example over fees.

questions.explanation: The people do not want to be tricked about the fees.

questions.question: Complete: 'Everyone's furious about the increase in car parking fees. We're all in the same ______ – we have no other option.'

steps: The idiom is 'in the same boat'.

questions.explanation: They share the same situation.

questions.question: According to the Active Vocabulary box, an idiom such as 'completely at sea' with a computer system means ...

steps: The example says 'completely at sea' means totally confused or not sure what to do.

questions.explanation: It is a figurative meaning.

questions.question: Which statement about idioms is TRUE according to the Active Vocabulary box?

options.A: they are used mainly in informal or colloquial language
options.B: they must always be used in formal essays
options.C: you can change the words in an idiom
options.D: you should use as many idioms as possible

questions.correct_answer_text: they are used mainly in informal or colloquial language

steps: The box says idioms are used mainly in informal or colloquial language.

questions.explanation: It is important not to change any word in an idiom.

questions.question: What is the LITERAL meaning of the verb 'fly'?

source.reference: Watch Out!: literal and figurative meanings

steps: Literally, to fly is to move through the air, like a bird.

questions.explanation: This is the literal meaning.

questions.question: What is the FIGURATIVE meaning of the verb 'fly'?

source.reference: Watch Out!: literal and figurative meanings

steps: Figuratively, to fly means to move quickly and suddenly, e.g. 'I flew down the platform'.

questions.explanation: I saw an opening in the crowd and flew down the platform.

questions.question: What does 'sailed through her interview' mean?

steps: 'Sail through' means to succeed at something easily.

questions.explanation: Reem sailed through her interview to become a tour guide.

questions.question: What does 'drives himself too hard' mean?

options.A: he works too much and pushes himself too far

questions.correct_answer_text: he works too much and pushes himself too far

steps: 'Drive yourself too hard' means to push yourself to work too much.

questions.explanation: He'll be ill if he's not careful.

questions.question: What does 'stumbled over some of the words' mean while reading a speech?

options.A: made mistakes or hesitated on the words

questions.correct_answer_text: made mistakes or hesitated on the words

steps: 'Stumble over words' means to make mistakes or hesitate while speaking or reading.

questions.explanation: He was so stressed that he made mistakes.

questions.question: What does 'we were staggered by the amount of work' mean?

steps: 'Be staggered by' means to be amazed or shocked by something.

questions.explanation: Here 'staggered' has a figurative meaning.

questions.question: What does 'I flew down the road to catch the bus' mean?

steps: 'Fly' here means to move quickly and suddenly.
solution.summary: flew down the road = went very quickly.

questions.explanation: He was late, so he ran quickly to catch the bus.

questions.question: What does 'let's just park that idea for now' mean?

options.A: let's leave that idea aside for now

questions.correct_answer_text: let's leave that idea aside for now

steps: 'Park an idea' means to leave it aside and come back to it later.
solution.summary: park an idea = set it aside.

questions.explanation: They cannot agree now, so they will return to it later.

questions.question: What does 'he jumped the lights' mean?

options.A: he drove through red traffic lights
options.B: he crossed the road at a crossing

questions.correct_answer_text: he drove through red traffic lights

steps: 'Jump the lights' means to drive through red traffic lights.
solution.summary: jumped the lights = drove through red lights.

questions.explanation: He was in such a hurry that he nearly crashed.

questions.question: What does 'he backpedalled very quickly' mean?

steps: 'Backpedal' here means to quickly change an opinion or decision.

questions.explanation: He changed his attitude when he realised they were police officers.

questions.question: Why should you NOT overuse idioms?

steps: The box says 'It is better not to overuse idioms, as this can sound unnatural.'

questions.explanation: Use idioms in the right places.

questions.question: What happens if you change a word in an idiom?

steps: The box says 'It is important not to change any word in an idiom or the meaning is lost.'

questions.explanation: Idioms must keep all their words.

questions.question: In 'I saw an opening in the crowd and flew down the platform', 'flew' is used ...

options.A: figuratively, meaning moved quickly and suddenly
options.B: literally, meaning flew like a bird

questions.correct_answer_text: figuratively, meaning moved quickly and suddenly

source.reference: Watch Out!: literal and figurative meanings

steps: Here 'flew' has its figurative meaning: to move quickly and suddenly.

questions.explanation: He is not flying like a bird; he is moving fast.
